questions.stem: A note asks why coal is a stock resource but sunlight is a flow resource. Explain briefly.

answer.exemplar: Coal exists as a finite accumulated stock that is depleted when used, while sunlight arrives continuously as a flow that cannot be stored as stock without conversion. The distinction is accumulation versus continuous arrival.

questions.explanation: Stock resources are accumulated and depletable; flow resources arrive continuously. Coal and sunlight illustrate that contrast.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: Stage 1: A resource is extracted faster than it regenerates. Stage 2: A planner calls it a flow resource. Is that correct?

options.text: No, it is being treated as a stock

questions.explanation: When extraction exceeds regeneration, the resource behaves as a stock being depleted. Calling it a flow resource ignores the rate mismatch.
questions.hint: Rate mismatch makes it a stock.

stimulus.body: On the note, a country's ratio rises from 0.1 to 0.3 without new discoveries. A planner attributes this to improved extraction technology.

questions.stem: Is the planner's attribution plausible?

options.text: No, only new discoveries raise the ratio
Yes, better technology can convert resources to reserves
No, the ratio cannot change without discoveries
Yes, but only if prices fall

questions.explanation: Improved technology can make previously uneconomic resources recoverable, converting resources to reserves and raising the ratio without new discoveries.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Land-use change under an agribusiness contract
questions.stem: On the note, an agribusiness contract converts forest to soy and displaces smallholders. Explain the combined land-use effect.

answer.exemplar: The contract converts prime forest to soy directly, while displaced smallholders clear additional forest elsewhere. The combined effect is larger than the contract area because indirect conversion adds to direct conversion.

questions.explanation: Direct conversion plus displaced clearing produces a larger total land-use change than the contract area alone. Both effects must be counted.
